topic: Fluid Resuscitation in Sepsis — How Much, What Fluid, and When to Stop
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Department of Intensive Care Medicine
speakerBio: An intensivist who has run fluid-responsiveness research for fifteen years and is quietly evangelical about the passive leg raise. His refrain: the second litre must be earned, not assumed.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

A 58-year-old with septic shock has had her 30 mL/kg. She's still mottled, MAP 62, lactate 4.1. The bedside nurse asks the question that separates good resuscitation from harm: "More fluid?" A reflex "yes, keep it going" has drowned more septic patients than any missed antibiotic. This session is about the hardest skill in sepsis — knowing how much, which fluid, and when to stop.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

Fluid is a drug: it has a dose, a therapeutic window, and a toxic overdose. The first 30 mL/kg is empiric; everything after that must be earned by proving the patient will actually respond.

2 · The 30 mL/kg starting point — where it comes from and its limits 💧

The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends an initial 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion (hypotension or lactate ≥4). Understand its status honestly: this is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence — a pragmatic, one-size starting dose to rapidly restore preload in a patient who is intravascularly depleted from capillary leak. It is a floor to begin with, not a target every patient must reach and certainly not a licence to keep going. Some patients (cardiac, renal failure, obviously fluid-overloaded) need less and earlier reassessment; the number is a default, not a dogma.

💡 One-liner

The 30 mL/kg is the opening bid, not the whole auction. After it, you stop guessing and start measuring — every further bolus must answer the question "is this patient still fluid-responsive?"

3 · Why 'keep giving fluid' kills — the two-hit model 🌊

Recall Session 1: sepsis sheds the glycocalyx and opens the endothelium, so infused fluid does not stay in the vessels — it leaks into the interstitium. Pour in more than the circulation can use and you get:

  • Tissue & pulmonary oedema → worsening gas exchange, longer ventilation.
  • Gut oedema & raised intra-abdominal pressure → ileus, abdominal compartment syndrome.
  • Renal congestion → the venous back-pressure impairs kidney perfusion; over-resuscitation is a cause of AKI, not a cure.
  • Glycocalyx damage — aggressive boluses (and rapid volume/atrial stretch releasing natriuretic peptides) can themselves further degrade the glycocalyx, worsening leak.

Observational data are consistent: a positive cumulative fluid balance in sepsis is associated with higher mortality. Fluid is resuscitation on the first hit and poison on the second.

4 · Dynamic assessment — replacing 'more?' with 'will it work?' 🔬

Static numbers (CVP, a single blood pressure) do not predict whether a bolus will raise cardiac output — CVP was abandoned as a resuscitation target for exactly this reason. Instead, use dynamic tests of fluid responsiveness, which ask whether increasing preload actually increases stroke volume (i.e. whether the patient sits on the steep part of the Frank–Starling curve):

TestWhat it doesPositive result
Passive leg raise (PLR)Tilts ~300 mL of venous blood from the legs centrally — a reversible, internal fluid challenge. Best all-rounder; works even in arrhythmia and spontaneous breathing.Stroke volume / cardiac output rises ≥10% → fluid-responsive
Stroke-volume variation (SVV) / pulse-pressure variation (PPV)Uses heart–lung interaction on a ventilator to gauge preload dependence.Variation >13% → fluid-responsive (only valid if sinus rhythm, fully ventilated, tidal volume ~8 mL/kg, no spontaneous effort)
Ultrasound / IVCEcho for stroke-volume change; IVC diameter and its respiratory collapsibility/distensibility.High collapsibility (spont.) or distensibility (ventilated); rising VTI with a bolus/PLR
Capillary refill time (CRT)Simple peripheral perfusion marker — press the fingertip, time the refill.Normalising CRT (<3 s) is a valid resuscitation target (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK)
🎯 Trial punchline — ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (JAMA 2019)

Resuscitating septic shock to a capillary refill time target was at least as good as — and in secondary analyses trended better than — chasing lactate clearance, with less fluid given and less organ dysfunction. The lesson: a simple perfusion endpoint at the bedside can outperform a blunt "drive the lactate down with volume" strategy. Peripheral perfusion, not just a number, guides you.

💡 Pearl — only half of patients respond

At any moment only about 50% of haemodynamically unstable patients are actually fluid-responsive. Give a bolus without checking and you have a coin-flip chance of doing nothing but adding to the flood. Dynamic testing turns a coin-flip into a decision.

5 · Which fluid? Balanced crystalloid over saline ⚖️

0.9% "normal" saline is neither normal nor benign: with 154 mmol/L of chloride it drives a hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis and renal afferent vasoconstriction. Balanced solutions (Hartmann's / Ringer's lactate / Plasma-Lyte) have a more physiological electrolyte profile. The trials:

TrialComparisonPunchline
SMART (NEJM 2018)Balanced vs saline, ~15,000 ICU patientsBalanced reduced the composite of death, new renal-replacement therapy, or persistent renal dysfunction (MAKE30); benefit most evident in sepsis.
BaSICS (JAMA 2021)Balanced (Plasma-Lyte) vs saline, BrazilNo overall mortality difference; signals of possible benefit in some subgroups — reassured that balanced is at least as safe.
PLUS (NEJM 2022)Balanced vs saline, ~5,000 ICU patients, AustralasiaNo significant difference in 90-day mortality overall.

Individually the large RCTs are not unanimous on mortality, but meta-analysis and mechanism point the same way, and SSC 2021 suggests balanced crystalloids over 0.9% saline for resuscitation. Given identical cost and a plausible signal of renal benefit with no evidence of harm, balanced is the sensible default — reserve saline for specific indications (e.g. hypochloraemic alkalosis, some traumatic brain-injury protocols).

⚔️ Contrast pair — balanced vs 0.9% saline

0.9% saline: Na 154 / Cl 154, supraphysiological chloride → hyperchloraemic acidosis, renal vasoconstriction. Balanced (Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte): chloride near-physiological (~98–111), buffer (lactate/acetate/gluconate), electrolytes close to plasma. In large sepsis/ICU data (SMART), balanced improved renal outcomes; SSC 2021 prefers balanced. Same volume, better chemistry.

6 · Colloids — starch, albumin, and what to avoid 🚫

  • Hydroxyethyl starch (HES): do not use. The CHEST (NEJM 2012) and 6S (NEJM 2012) trials showed starch caused more acute kidney injury and more renal-replacement therapy (6S also showed increased mortality) versus crystalloid. Starch is contraindicated in sepsis — a closed question.
  • Albumin: not first-line, but has a role. The SAFE trial (NEJM 2004) showed albumin was safe and as effective as saline overall (with a signal of harm in traumatic brain injury). ALBIOS (NEJM 2014) showed no overall mortality benefit from adding albumin to crystalloid, with a hint of benefit in the septic-shock subgroup. SSC 2021 suggests albumin may be added in patients who have received large volumes of crystalloid — as an adjunct, not a replacement.

7 · When to stop — and when to actively remove fluid 🛑

The modern framing is the four dynamic phases of fluid therapy — "ROSE":

PhaseR·O·S·EFluid strategy
1. ResuscitationRescueRapid boluses to save a life — the Hour-1 setting. Minutes.
2. OptimisationOptimiseTitrated fluid guided by dynamic responsiveness; give only if it will raise output. Hours.
3. StabilisationStabiliseMaintenance only; the patient no longer needs boluses. Aim for neutral balance. Days.
4. EvacuationEvacuateDe-resuscitation — actively achieve a negative balance (diuretics ± ultrafiltration) to clear accumulated oedema.

De-resuscitation — the deliberate removal of the fluid you gave — is now recognised as part of good sepsis care. Once the shock is resolved and the capillary leak seals, the litres that saved the patient become the litres congesting their lungs, gut, and kidneys. Getting patients into a negative balance in the recovery phase is associated with better outcomes. The full arc of care is: fill fast, then optimise carefully, then stabilise, then take it back off.

☠️ M&M — "She was still hypotensive, so we kept giving fluid"

A 58-year-old with pyelonephritic septic shock received her 30 mL/kg, remained at MAP 60, and over the next four hours was given a further five litres of saline by a rotating team, each member reaching for another bolus because "the pressure's still soft." Nobody performed a passive leg raise; nobody started noradrenaline. By morning she was in florid pulmonary oedema on 60% oxygen, hyperchloraemic (Cl 118) with a worsening acidosis, anuric, and intubated for a fluid-overload ARDS picture. A PLR at hour two would have shown she was not fluid-responsive; the correct move after the first 30 mL/kg was noradrenaline and balanced fluid titrated to a dynamic endpoint, not five more litres of saline. Lesson: persistent hypotension is an indication to test responsiveness and start a pressor, not to keep pouring. Fluid without a dynamic answer, and saline instead of balanced, harmed this patient twice.

8 · A practical fluid algorithm 🧭

  1. Resuscitate: 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4, begun immediately.
  2. Before every further bolus, test responsiveness — PLR (≥10% SV rise), SVV/PPV >13% if ventilated, IVC/echo, or trend CRT.
  3. Responsive? Give a small, defined bolus (e.g. 250–500 mL) and re-test. Not responsive? Stop fluid; start/uptitrate noradrenaline to MAP ≥65.
  4. Consider albumin as an adjunct after large crystalloid volumes; never use starch.
  5. Track perfusion targets: falling lactate, normalising CRT, urine output, mentation.
  6. De-resuscitate: once stable and leak resolved, move to neutral then negative balance (ROSE phases 3–4).

9 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • Fluid is a drug with a toxic overdose; 30 mL/kg is the opening bid, not the whole treatment.
  • After the first bolus, measure — don't guess: PLR, SVV/PPV, IVC/echo, CRT. Only ~50% of patients are fluid-responsive.
  • Balanced crystalloid > 0.9% saline (SMART renal benefit; BaSICS/PLUS neutral but safe) — SSC 2021 prefers balanced.
  • No starch, ever (CHEST, 6S — AKI and death); albumin as an adjunct after large volumes (SAFE/ALBIOS).
  • Over-resuscitation harms: pulmonary/gut oedema, renal congestion, higher mortality with positive balance.
  • ROSE phases: Resuscitation → Optimisation → Stabilisation → Evacuation. Know when to stop and when to de-resuscitate.

That closes the loop on Day 1: we have traced sepsis from the shed glycocalyx, to its definition, to the golden hour, to the fluid that both saves and drowns. Master the mechanism, and every number on the guideline writes itself.

moderatorQs.q: The 30 mL/kg initial bolus is one of the most debated numbers in sepsis. How should a trainee understand its evidence base and its limits?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: They should understand it is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence — a pragmatic, standardised starting dose to rapidly restore preload in a patient made intravascularly dry by capillary leak, not a physiologically validated target. Its value is as a fast, unambiguous default that prevents under-resuscitation in the chaotic first hour. Its danger is being treated as a mandate: patients with cardiac or renal impairment, or evident overload, need less and earlier reassessment. The correct mental model is that 30 mL/kg is the opening bid, after which you switch from an empiric protocol to individualised, dynamically-guided titration — every subsequent bolus justified by a demonstrated fluid-responsive state rather than a body-weight formula.

moderatorQs.q: Summarise the balanced-crystalloid-versus-saline evidence and give us your bottom line for practice.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: SMART (NEJM 2018, ~15,000 patients) found balanced solutions reduced the composite of death, new renal-replacement therapy or persistent renal dysfunction (MAKE30), with the signal strongest in sepsis. BaSICS (2021) and PLUS (2022) each found no significant overall mortality difference, but neither showed balanced to be worse — they establish safety and equipoise on hard mortality. Mechanistically, 0.9% saline's supraphysiological chloride (154 mmol/L) causes hyperchloraemic acidosis and renal afferent vasoconstriction, which balanced fluids avoid. Bottom line: SSC 2021 suggests balanced crystalloids over saline, and given identical cost, a plausible renal benefit, and no evidence of harm, balanced (Hartmann's/Plasma-Lyte) is the default — with saline reserved for specific indications like hypochloraemic alkalosis or certain neuro protocols.

moderatorQs.q: What is 'de-resuscitation,' and where does it sit in the overall arc of fluid management?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: De-resuscitation is the deliberate, active removal of accumulated fluid once the shock has resolved and the capillary leak has sealed — using diuretics and, if needed, ultrafiltration to drive a negative fluid balance. It occupies the last two of the four ROSE phases: after Resuscitation (rescue boluses) and Optimisation (dynamically-guided titration) come Stabilisation (maintenance, neutral balance) and Evacuation (negative balance). It matters because a persistently positive cumulative balance in sepsis is associated with higher mortality, prolonged ventilation and AKI — the very litres that rescued the patient become the oedema congesting their lungs, gut and kidneys. Good fluid care is therefore a full arc: fill fast, optimise carefully, stabilise, then take it back off.

audienceQs.q: Which single test of fluid responsiveness should I reach for at the bedside, and why?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The passive leg raise (PLR) is the best all-round bedside test. Lowering the trunk and raising the legs auto-transfuses roughly 300 mL of venous blood centrally — a reversible, internal fluid challenge that gives no fluid if the answer is 'no.' A rise in stroke volume or cardiac output of ≥10% (measured by echo VTI, an arterial waveform device, or end-tidal CO₂ as a surrogate) means the patient is fluid-responsive. Its great advantage over SVV/PPV is that it remains valid in arrhythmia, spontaneous breathing, and low tidal volumes, where the respiratory-variation indices fail. Remember only about half of unstable patients are responsive at any moment, so the PLR converts a coin-flip bolus into an evidence-based decision. Just measure a real output signal — a blood-pressure change alone is unreliable.

audienceQs.q: Is it ever okay to just give more fluid if the blood pressure is still low, without doing all these tests?
audienceQs.answerHTML: After the initial 30 mL/kg, no — repeated blind boluses for a persistently low pressure is exactly how patients are harmed. Persistent hypotension after the first bolus is an indication to do two things: test fluid responsiveness (a passive leg raise takes a minute) and, if the patient is not clearly responsive, start noradrenaline to defend a MAP ≥65. Only about 50% of unstable patients will actually raise their cardiac output with more fluid; in the other half you are just adding to pulmonary and tissue oedema, worsening the capillary leak, and congesting the kidneys. So the honest rule is: the first 30 mL/kg is empiric, but every litre after that must be earned by evidence it will help.

audienceQs.q: Where do albumin and the starch solutions sit in sepsis resuscitation?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Starch (hydroxyethyl starch) is contraindicated in sepsis — the CHEST and 6S trials showed it causes more acute kidney injury and renal-replacement therapy, with 6S also showing increased mortality. It should not be used. Albumin is a different story: it is safe (SAFE trial, though avoid in traumatic brain injury) but not first-line. ALBIOS showed no overall mortality benefit from adding albumin to crystalloid, with only a hint of benefit in the septic-shock subgroup. So SSC 2021 positions albumin as an adjunct that may be added in patients who have already received large volumes of crystalloid — never as the primary resuscitation fluid, which remains balanced crystalloid. Practically: reach for balanced crystalloid first, consider albumin after several litres, and never stock starch for sepsis.
